tasks.q: Step through a binary search for 23. Tap each item the algorithm checks, in order.
tasks.fb: Three checks on a nine-item list: the middle, then the middle of what is left, and so on.
tasks.title: Binary search: find 23

tasks.q: Which item does a binary search look at first?
tasks.fb: Starting in the middle is what makes it possible to discard half.

tasks.q: Why must the list be sorted?
a: Comparing with the middle only tells you which half to keep if the order is known
Because it is faster to read
Because sorted lists use less memory
tasks.fb: Unsorted, the comparison tells you nothing about where the target is.

tasks.q: When is sorting first, then binary searching, worth the effort?
a: When the same list will be searched many times
tasks.fb: Pay the sorting cost once, save on every search afterwards.

tasks.q: A sorted list has 1,000,000 items. Roughly how many checks does a binary search need?
tasks.fb: Each check halves it: 20 halvings gets you from a million to one.

tasks.q: A list doubles in size. What happens to a binary search?
a: It takes four times as long
tasks.fb: That is why it copes with enormous data.

tasks.q: Does each statement describe a linear search or a binary search?
items: Works on a list in any order
About 20 checks for a million items
Up to a million checks for a million items
tasks.fb: Four rows of this table are the most common exam question on searching.

tasks.q: Which search would you use on 30 items that are constantly reordered?
a: Linear, because keeping them sorted would cost more than it saves
tasks.fb: The cost of sorting has to be counted too.

tasks.q: Put these lines into a working binary search.
steps: left = 0 and right = the last index
while left is less than or equal to right
if list[mid] is the target then stop, found
if the target is larger, set left = mid + 1
tasks.fb: Two pointers closing in on the answer.

tasks.q: Why is DIV, or integer division, used for the midpoint?
a: An index must be a whole number
It is faster than normal division

tasks.q: Find 66 with a binary search. Tap each item the algorithm checks.
tasks.fb: The target at the far end still takes only a few checks, because each one halves the list.
tasks.title: Binary search: find 66

tasks.q: Which is the strongest description of a binary search?
a: On a sorted list, it compares the middle item with the target and discards the half that cannot contain it, repeating until found
It splits the list in half

tasks.fb: Each tap must be the midpoint of what is left after the previous discard.
tasks.title: Binary search: find 19

tasks.q: Which search suits each situation better?
items: A sorted phone directory of a million entries
A list rebuilt from scratch every second
A sorted list of ten thousand product codes
tasks.fb: Sorted and large points to binary; unsorted or changing points to linear.

info.title: The dictionary method
info.text: Opening a dictionary in the middle and deciding which half to keep is a binary search. Most people do it without being taught.

info.title: Famously hard to write
info.text: A study found most programmers write a buggy binary search on the first attempt, usually getting the midpoint or the pointers wrong.

info.title: Twenty questions
info.text: The game works because twenty yes/no questions can distinguish about a million possibilities, exactly the binary search maths.

info.title: Big O
info.text: At A level this is O(log n): the work grows with the logarithm of the list size, which is why it barely grows at all.

info.title: Databases do this
info.text: A database index exists precisely so that searches can halve the data instead of scanning it.

info.title: Exam tip
info.text: If you forget to say the list must be sorted, you are likely to drop a mark, whatever else you write.

diagrams.title: Run both on the same list
diagrams.text: Linear and binary search side by side on one list, with the comparisons counted. Then the catch: binary needs it sorted first.
